lesson.title: The Numbers That Never Change: Meeting Constants
lesson.summary: Explains a constant as a fixed numerical value in an expression, contrasts it with variables, and shows how to spot constants in real situations like a flat fee.
lesson.body:
A constant is a number whose value never changes within a given problem. It sits in an expression as a fixed quantity, unlike a variable, which can stand for different numbers depending on the situation. In the expression x + 7, the 7 is a constant. No matter what number x happens to be, that 7 always means exactly seven, nothing more and nothing less. Recognizing constants is one of the first steps toward reading an algebraic expression the way a mathematician does: some pieces are fixed, and some pieces are free to vary.

It helps to think about where constants come from in real situations. A flat fee, a starting amount, a fixed rate that never depends on the problem's changing quantity, these are all constants in disguise. If a taxi ride costs a flat $3 just to get in the cab, plus $2 per mile, the 3 is a constant: it is charged no matter how far you travel. The $2 per mile is different; it gets multiplied by the number of miles, which can vary, so it plays a different role that we will name a coefficient in the next section. For now, the key distinction is simple: a constant stands alone, unattached to any variable.

Numbers can also be constants even when there is a minus sign in front of them rather than a plus sign. In the expression 5x squared minus 9, the negative 9 is the constant. It's worth noticing that a constant keeps its sign as part of its identity: we say the constant is negative 9, not that we are subtracting a constant of positive 9 from the rest of the expression.

It is also worth noticing that constants do not require a variable to be present at all. An expression like 12 + 7 is made up of two constants and nothing else; since neither number is attached to a letter, evaluating the expression always gives the same result, 19, no matter what problem you are working on. Some constants are so important that they get their own special symbol and turn up in the same fixed form across many different formulas; pi, approximately 3.14159, is one famous example, always representing the same fixed ratio no matter which circle you are measuring.

Let's work through an example to make this concrete. A savings account starts with $50 already in it, an amount that never changes for this problem, and gains $4 each week from an allowance. If w represents the number of weeks, the total savings is 50 + 4w. Here, 50 is the constant, and 4 is attached to the variable w. Evaluate the total after 6 weeks by substituting w = 6: 50 + 4(6). Multiply first: 4 times 6 is 24. Then add: 50 + 24 = 74. So after 6 weeks, the account holds $74, and the 50 dollars the account started with is exactly the constant we identified, unaffected by how many weeks pass.

Constants matter because they anchor an expression to something fixed and knowable, while variables carry the part of the situation that can shift. Once you can pick out which pieces of an expression are constants and which are attached to variables, you're ready to look at coefficients, which describe exactly how a variable is being scaled.
